claim: A command hook that exits 1 (the conventional Unix failure code) without valid JSON does not block anything; only exit 2 blocks.
why: Exit 1 is a non-blocking error unless the hook sets onFailure block, so the action goes ahead.
check: Look for enforcement hooks whose scripts exit 1 (or use set -e style failures) to deny; those never block and should exit 2 or print a deny decision.
quote: even though 1 is the conventional Unix failure code. If your hook is meant to enforce a policy, use `exit 2`.

claim: Exit code 2 blocks even when the hook also prints JSON; the JSON fields are still read but cannot override the block, including a permissionDecision of allow.
why: Mixing exit codes and JSON is unsupported; exit 2 keeps its blocking effect.
check: Flag hooks that exit 2 and also print an allow or updatedInput expecting it to take effect.
quote: Exit 2 blocks even when your hook prints JSON:

claim: On exit 0, Claude never sees the hook's stderr; to show a warning to Claude from PostToolUse or PostToolUseFailure the hook must exit 2.
why: Stderr only reaches Claude on blocking exit codes where the event honors it.
check: Flag hooks that echo guidance to stderr and exit 0 expecting Claude to read it.
quote: Claude never sees stderr from a hook that exits 0.

claim: For PermissionRequest hooks, exit 2 is not honored: the permission flow proceeds unchanged and stderr is discarded, so denial must come from a decision object in JSON.
why: PermissionRequest is not a blockable event by exit code.
check: Flag PermissionRequest hooks that deny by exit 2; they do not deny.
quote: A hook that exits 2 without a `decision` object leaves the permission flow unchanged, and its stderr is discarded.

claim: By default a hook that fails to start, errors, or times out lets the action proceed; onFailure block (command and http hooks, v2.1.295+) makes failure block.
why: A wrong script path in settings.json otherwise means the policy never runs.
check: For each policy hook that must always hold, confirm onFailure is block (or the script cannot fail silently) and that the script path exists.
quote: A policy hook with a wrong path or a crashing script then lets everything through.

claim: A PreToolUse hook that times out does not block the tool call; it falls through to the normal permission flow unless onFailure is block.
why: Timeouts discard the hook's output so no decision is rendered.
check: Flag slow PreToolUse gate hooks without onFailure block or a tight timeout.
quote: so don't count on a stalled hook to act as a gate.

claim: Default hook timeouts are 600 seconds for command, http and mcp_tool, 30 for prompt, and 60 for agent hooks.
why: The defaults differ by handler type and some events lower them.
check: Flag hooks with no timeout that run slow work on every tool call, and prompt hooks that need more than 30 seconds.
quote: Defaults: 600 for `command`, `http`, and `mcp_tool`; 30 for `prompt`; 60 for `agent`.

claim: UserPromptSubmit command, http and mcp_tool hooks default to a 30 second timeout (not 600), and a timed-out hook's output, including additionalContext, is dropped while the prompt still goes through.
why: The hook runs before every prompt and blocks processing, so a stuck hook stalls the session.
check: Check UserPromptSubmit hooks that do network or heavy work; they may silently lose their context injection.
quote: `UserPromptSubmit` hooks have a default timeout of 30 seconds for `command`, `http`, and `mcp_tool` types, shorter than the 600-second default for those types on most other events.

claim: The hook if filter is best effort: when Claude Code cannot split a Bash command into subcommands it runs the hook regardless, and a hard allow or deny should use the permission system rather than a hook if filter.
why: The source says the if filter is best-effort.
check: Flag setups that rely on a hook if pattern or a hook alone as the only barrier for a must-never command.
quote: When Claude Code can't split the Bash input into subcommands, it runs your hook regardless of the pattern.

claim: A hook returning allow does not override matching deny or ask rules: deny and ask rules are still evaluated regardless of what the hook returns.
why: Permission rules keep deny-first precedence over PreToolUse decisions.
check: Do not credit a hook allow as defeating a deny rule, and do not expect a hook to loosen a managed deny.
quote: are still evaluated regardless of what the hook returns

claim: When several PreToolUse hooks disagree, the precedence is deny over defer over ask over allow.
why: The most restrictive answer wins.
check: A single deny among multiple hooks is enough to block; check no hook is expected to override another's deny.
quote: When multiple PreToolUse hooks return different decisions, precedence is `deny` > `defer` > `ask` > `allow`.

claim: PreToolUse hooks do not fire for files referenced with @ in a prompt, because their contents are inserted while building the prompt, so a Read-matching hook does not guard them.
why: No tool call happens for @ mentions.
check: If a rule says certain files must never be read, require a Read deny rule (or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FILE_MENTIONS) rather than only a Read hook.
quote: Claude Code inserts their contents while building the prompt, so no PreToolUse hook fires for them, including hooks matching `Read`.

claim: A user typing /skillname bypasses PreToolUse matching on the Skill tool; UserPromptExpansion is the event that covers that direct path.
why: PreToolUse on Skill fires only when Claude calls the tool.
check: Flag skill-gating hooks that use only a PreToolUse Skill matcher.
quote: but typing `/skillname` directly bypasses `PreToolUse`.

claim: Claude Code overrides a Stop hook after eight consecutive continuations, so a Stop hook that keeps blocking must check stop_hook_active or it will be cut off.
why: The cap prevents infinite Stop loops; it resets when Claude calls a tool and can be raised with CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP.
check: Check Stop hooks that block on a condition for a stop_hook_active guard and note a must-hold condition is not guaranteed past eight blocks.
quote: after stop hooks have continued the turn eight times in a row, Claude Code overrides the next block and ends the turn.

claim: PostToolUse hooks cannot block or undo; the tool has already run, and updatedToolOutput only changes what Claude sees, not the side effects or telemetry.
why: The hook fires after execution.
check: Flag PostToolUse hooks used as guards for something that must not happen; move them to PreToolUse.
quote: `updatedToolOutput` only changes what Claude sees. The tool has already run by the time the hook fires

claim: Async command hooks cannot block or control Claude; decision, permissionDecision and continue have no effect.
why: The action they would control has already completed.
check: Flag enforcement hooks marked async: true.
quote: Async hooks can't block or control Claude's behavior: response fields like `decision`, `permissionDecision`, and `continue` have no effect

claim: A synchronous hook's stdout must be exactly one JSON object for the JSON to be parsed; extra text such as a shell-profile echo makes it plain text and the decision is silently ignored.
why: Parsing requires the output to start with an opening brace and nothing else around it.
check: Check hook scripts and shell profiles for stray stdout before the JSON; a hook exiting 0 with ignored JSON shows no error.
quote: Print nothing but the JSON object to stdout.

claim: additionalContext, systemMessage, initialUserMessage and plain stdout from a hook are each capped at 10,000 characters; over the cap the output is saved to a file and only a preview of up to 2,000 characters is injected.
why: Claude Code does not ask Claude to read the overflow file.
check: Flag SessionStart or UserPromptSubmit hooks that inject large blobs that Claude must always see.
quote: A hook's `additionalContext`, `systemMessage`, and `initialUserMessage` strings, and its plain stdout, are capped at 10,000 characters:

claim: For instructions that never change, use CLAUDE.md rather than a hook that injects them; reserve additionalContext for dynamic state.
why: CLAUDE.md loads without running a script.
check: Flag SessionStart hooks that only echo static conventions.
quote: It loads without running a script and is the standard place for static project conventions.

claim: Write hook-injected context as factual statements, not imperative system-style commands, or Claude may treat it as prompt injection and surface it instead of using it.
why: Out-of-band command phrasing triggers prompt-injection defenses.
check: Review additionalContext strings written as commands like IGNORE or YOU MUST from the system.
quote: Text framed as out-of-band system commands can trigger Claude's prompt-injection defenses, which causes Claude to surface the text to you instead of treating it as context.

claim: An MCP server matcher needs a regex tail: mcp__memory alone is an exact string and matches no tool, so mcp__memory__.* is required; plugin-bundled servers use a scoped server segment.
why: Matchers with only letters, digits, underscore and hyphen are compared as exact strings.
check: Flag MCP hook matchers without .* or written against a plugin server's bare key.
quote: The `.*` is required: a matcher like `mcp__memory` or `mcp__brave-search` contains only exact-match characters, so it is compared as an exact string and matches no tool.

claim: On Windows, file_path in hook input uses backslashes, so a forward-slash path comparison never matches and the call proceeds unblocked.
why: Paths arrive in native format, absolute.
check: Check path-guard hooks for separator normalization.
quote: A comparison written with forward slashes, such as a `/src/` check, never matches a backslash path, and the tool call proceeds as if the hook had nothing to block

claim: A PostToolUse hook matching Edit|Write does not fire when a Bash command or outside process rewrites the file; FileChanged is the event for that.
why: PostToolUse is tied to the tool that ran.
check: Flag format/lint/guard hooks on Edit|Write that assume they see all file changes.
quote: Claude Code doesn't run a `PostToolUse` hook matching `Edit|Write` when a `Bash` command or a process outside Claude Code rewrites the same file.

claim: In -p and SDK sessions Claude Code never shows the trust dialog and treats the folder as trusted, so hooks in a repository's .claude/settings.json run in a folder you have never trusted.
why: There is no dialog to accept in non-interactive mode.
check: For CI running claude -p over untrusted repos, check for --bare or disableAllHooks.
quote: Claude Code never shows the dialog and treats the folder as trusted, so hooks committed in a repository's `.claude/settings.json` run in a folder you've never trusted

claim: Hook entries merge across settings levels, and disableAllHooks from non-managed settings cannot disable managed hooks.
why: Managed hooks are admin-controlled.
check: Do not expect a project or user setting to remove an organization hook.
quote: Hook entries merge across settings levels rather than replacing each other: user, project, and local settings add their own hooks without removing managed ones

claim: Hooks run for tool calls inside subagents, with agent_id and agent_type in the input.
why: Settings, managed and plugin hooks apply to subagent tool calls the same as the main conversation.
check: Subagents do not need separate copies of settings-level guard hooks.
quote: When a subagent calls a tool, tool events such as `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse` fire the same configured hooks as in the main conversation

claim: For prompt hooks, ok false on PreToolUse denies the call and by default ends the turn unless continueOnBlock is true; agent hooks are experimental and prompt/agent hooks are LLM judgments, not deterministic.
why: The doc says to prefer command hooks for production workflows.
check: Flag prompt or agent hooks used for hard rules that a command hook could enforce deterministically.
quote: Agent hooks are experimental. Behavior and configuration may change in future releases.

claim: ConfigChange hooks can block settings changes with exit 2 or a block decision, except policy_settings changes, which can never be blocked.
why: Enterprise-managed settings must always take effect.
check: A ConfigChange hook cannot protect managed settings; it can protect user, project, local and skills files.
quote: `policy_settings` changes can't be blocked.

claim: A PreToolUse deny holds in every permission mode, including bypassPermissions and dontAsk, so hooks can enforce policy users cannot bypass by changing mode.
why: PreToolUse fires before any permission-mode check.
check: Prefer a PreToolUse deny hook (or deny rule) for must-hold rules over prose in CLAUDE.md.
quote: This lets you enforce policy that users can't bypass by changing their permission mode.

claim: Hooks give deterministic control: actions always happen instead of relying on the LLM to choose to run them.
why: This is the stated reason to use hooks over instructions.
check: Where a rule must always hold (format after edit, block a file), expect a hook or permission rule, not a prose instruction.
quote: which gives you deterministic control: certain actions always happen rather than relying on the LLM to choose to run them.

claim: When multiple hooks match an event they run in parallel; one hook's deny does not stop sibling hooks' side effects.
why: All commands run to completion before results are merged.
check: Do not rely on an earlier hook's deny to suppress a logging or side-effect hook.
quote: One hook returning `deny` doesn't stop sibling hooks from executing.

claim: When several PreToolUse hooks return updatedInput for the same tool, the rewrites are not merged and which one wins is not guaranteed.
why: No merge or ordering guarantee exists.
check: Flag more than one hook rewriting the same tool's input.
quote: Claude Code doesn't merge the rewrites or guarantee which rewrite the tool runs with.

claim: Putting permissionDecision or additionalContext at the top level instead of inside hookSpecificOutput parses fine but is silently ignored.
why: Field placement is event-specific.
check: Check hook JSON for fields at the wrong level.
quote: Claude Code ignores the misplaced fields without reporting an error.

claim: A hook protecting files via Edit and Write matchers does not stop Claude changing the same files with shell commands; add deny rules and sandboxing.
why: The hook only sees the matched tools.
check: For must-protect files, expect Edit deny rules plus sandbox filesystem limits besides the hook.
quote: Claude can still change the protected files with shell commands.

claim: Settings precedence is managed, then command line (--settings), then project local, then shared project, then user; higher overrides the same key lower.
why: Per-key override by level; environment variables are not a level.
check: When a setting seems ignored, check each level and which one sets it.
quote: Settings precedence, highest first: managed settings, command line, project local, shared project, user.

claim: List settings such as permissions.allow merge across files instead of overriding; fallbackModel, modelPicker, availableModels (managed) and modelSettings are exceptions.
why: Each file can add entries without removing another file's.
check: Do not assume a project file can remove a user or managed allow entry.
quote: Claude Code combines the lists instead of picking one, so each file can add entries without removing another file's.

claim: permissions.defaultMode values auto and bypassPermissions do not take effect from project or local settings.
why: A cloned repository must not start sessions in those modes.
check: Flag defaultMode auto or bypassPermissions in .claude/settings.json; it silently does nothing.
quote: values `auto` and `bypassPermissions` don't take effect from project or local settings

claim: Project permissions.allow rules wait for each teammate to trust the folder, but deny and ask rules apply immediately.
why: Allow rules loosen restrictions; deny and ask only tighten.
check: Do not count on committed allow rules in non-interactive or untrusted contexts; deny rules are safe.
quote: `deny` and `ask` rules apply right away.

claim: --settings applies above user, project and local files and below managed settings.
why: It is per-session and writes no file.
check: Use it for one-off overrides, not to defeat managed policy.
quote: Claude Code applies it above your user, project, and local files and below managed settings.

claim: Settings files are strict JSON: a comment or trailing comma is an error, and a broken entry is skipped while the rest continues.
why: An invalid permission rule or hook name is dropped with a warning.
check: Validate settings JSON; a silently dropped deny rule or hook is a hole.
quote: Settings files are strict JSON: a `//` comment or a trailing comma is a syntax error

claim: Most settings edits, including permissions and hooks, apply to a running session without restart because Claude Code watches the files.
why: File watching reloads user, project, local and managed settings.
check: No restart is needed to test hook or permission changes.
quote: Claude Code watches your settings files and reloads them when they change, so it applies most edits to the running session without a restart

claim: Switching models mid-session makes the first request re-read the whole conversation uncached because each model has its own prompt cache.
why: Caches are per model.
check: Flag workflows that switch models often inside long sessions.
quote: Each model has its own prompt cache, so the first request after a switch re-reads the whole conversation uncached

claim: In user settings the effortLevel key is ignored by Opus 5.5 and later models, which start at their own default until a level is saved via /effort under modelSettings.
why: Per-model saved levels replaced the old key for newer models.
check: A user effortLevel in ~/.claude/settings.json does not control effort for Opus 5.5.
quote: Opus 5.5 and models released after it ignore it and start at their own default until you save a level for them

claim: alwaysThinkingEnabled false has no effect on models that always think, such as Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable models.
why: Thinking cannot be turned off on those models.
check: Do not credit alwaysThinkingEnabled false as a cost saving on those models; use effort instead.
quote: On models that always think, such as Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, and the Fable models, `false` has no effect.

claim: promptCacheTtl 1h keeps the cache warm across longer breaks but bills cache writes at a higher rate than 5m; subagentPromptCacheTtl covers subagents, compaction and helper requests separately.
why: The two keys cover different requests.
check: Check TTL settings against how often sessions pause.
quote: The one-hour lifetime keeps the cache warm across longer breaks, and the API

claim: bashOutputMaxChars is clamped to 4000 through 128000 characters and, when set, makes Claude Code ignore BASH_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH.
why: It sizes the inline ceiling and read-back window together.
check: Raising it trades context for fewer file reads.
quote: Claude Code clamps the value into the range `4000` to `128000`

claim: When the skill listing exceeds its budget (default 1% of context) Claude Code keeps every skill's name but drops descriptions of the least-used skills.
why: Skills lose discoverability, not availability.
check: Check skill count and description length against skillListingBudgetFraction and skillListingMaxDescChars (default 1536).
quote: keeps every skill's name but drops the descriptions of the least-used skills, so Claude can still invoke those skills but is less likely to choose one on its own.

claim: includeGitInstructions false removes both the built-in commit and PR instructions and the git status snapshot from context.
why: They load by default each session.
check: If the setup has its own git skills, check whether the built-in git instructions are duplicated.
quote: Set this key to `false` to leave both out, for example when you use your own git workflow skills.

claim: Only managed settings can disable managed hooks with disableAllHooks, and allowManagedHooksOnly blocks user, project, local and plugin hooks.
why: Admin control of hooks.
check: In a managed environment, user hooks may not run at all; check /hooks.
quote: Restrict hook execution to hooks your organization deploys.

claim: Permission rules are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow, and the first match decides regardless of specificity; an allow cannot carve an exception out of a deny.
why: Order is fixed, not specificity-based.
check: Flag allow rules intended as exceptions to a broader deny.
quote: Rules are evaluated in order: deny, then ask, then allow. The first match in that order determines the outcome, and rule specificity doesn't change the order.

claim: Permission rules are enforced by Claude Code, not the model; instructions in prompts or CLAUDE.md shape what Claude tries but do not change what is allowed.
why: Rules are harness enforcement.
check: A must-never rule written only in CLAUDE.md is not enforced; look for deny rules, hooks or sandbox.
quote: Permission rules are enforced by Claude Code, not by the model.

claim: A bare tool-name deny rule such as Bash removes the tool from Claude's context entirely, while a scoped rule like Bash(rm *) leaves the tool and blocks matching calls.
why: Bare deny also saves definition context.
check: Use bare deny for tools never needed; check scoped deny for must-block commands.
quote: A bare tool name like `Bash` removes the tool from Claude's context entirely, so Claude never sees it.

claim: A Bash deny or ask rule matches the command as written, so Bash(curl *) misses /usr/bin/curl and sh -c forms; it is not a security boundary.
why: Rules match command text only.
check: For must-hold network or file restrictions require the sandbox or a PreToolUse hook, not just a Bash deny rule.
quote: so a deny or ask rule covers the invocation Claude usually produces and isn't a security boundary around the program.

claim: Read and Edit deny rules do not cover commands that read files without naming them or arbitrary subprocesses; OS-level enforcement needs the sandbox.
why: They apply to built-in file tools, recognized Bash file commands and redirections.
check: Check that secret-file protection includes sandbox denyRead where scripts could read them.
quote: They don't apply to a command that reads files without naming them, such as `grep -r pattern .`

claim: A PreToolUse hook that exits 2 blocks before permission rules are evaluated, so the block holds even where an allow rule would approve; this pairs a broad Bash allow with a blocking hook.
why: Blocking hooks take precedence over allow rules.
check: Check that a broad allow is accompanied by blocking hooks or deny rules for the dangerous subset.
quote: A hook that exits with code 2 stops the tool call before permission rules are evaluated, so the block applies even when an allow rule would otherwise let the call proceed.

claim: In bypassPermissions mode allow rules have no effect, while deny rules still block; hook allows and actions no mode auto-approves still apply.
why: The mode skips prompts rather than consulting allow rules.
check: Flag bypassPermissions outside isolated containers or VMs.
quote: Allow rules have no effect in `bypassPermissions`.

claim: With Claude Code v2.1.283 or later, auto mode is the built-in starting permission mode for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions.
why: Default mode changed over versions.
check: Do not assume sessions start in Manual; check defaultMode and settings that disable auto mode.
quote: With Claude Code v2.1.283 or later, auto mode is the built-in starting permission mode for interactive terminal and VS Code sessions.

claim: claude -p and Agent SDK runs with no permission mode start in Manual mode (v2.1.302+), so calls needing approval are denied unless allowed by rule, hook, callback or permission-prompt-tool.
why: No prompt can be shown.
check: CI scripts need --allowedTools, --permission-mode auto or dontAsk with an allowlist.
quote: Calls needing approval are denied unless you approve them with an allow rule, hook, `canUseTool` callback, or `--permission-prompt-tool`.

claim: Auto mode pauses and resumes prompting after the classifier blocks 3 times in a row or 20 times total; the thresholds are not configurable.
why: Repeated blocks usually mean missing infrastructure context.
check: Where auto mode is used for long unattended runs, expect fallback to prompts or no-run in -p.
quote: if the classifier blocks an action 3 times in a row or 20 times total, auto mode pauses and Claude Code resumes prompting.

claim: dontAsk mode with an explicit allowlist is the recommended fit for CI and restricted environments.
why: The session never waits for input.
check: CI using bypassPermissions where dontAsk plus allowlist would do is over-permissive.
quote: Use this mode for CI pipelines or restricted environments where you pre-define what Claude may do; the session never waits for input.

claim: The sandbox is off by default and covers shell commands only; Read, Edit, Write, WebFetch, WebSearch, MCP servers and hooks run outside it.
why: File tools follow permission rules instead.
check: A sandbox denyRead or allowedDomains does not restrict the Read tool or WebFetch.
quote: The sandbox covers shell commands only. Claude's file tools, MCP servers, and hooks

claim: If the sandbox cannot start (unsupported platform or missing dependencies) Claude Code runs commands unsandboxed by default; sandbox.failIfUnavailable true makes it exit instead, and native Windows runs unsandboxed.
why: Fail-open default.
check: Where the sandbox is a security gate, check failIfUnavailable and allowUnsandboxedCommands false.
quote: By default, when the platform doesn't support the sandbox or the dependency check at startup fails, Claude Code runs commands without sandboxing.

claim: Claude may retry a sandbox-failed command with dangerouslyDisableSandbox, and a matching allow rule approves that retry without a prompt; allowUnsandboxedCommands false disables the retry.
why: The retry is an escape hatch.
check: Check for broad allow rules like Bash(curl *) that silently approve unsandboxed retries.
quote: Claude analyzes the failure and may retry the command with the `dangerouslyDisableSandbox` parameter.

claim: Allowing broad domains such as github.com in the sandbox can create exfiltration paths, since the proxy decides from the client-supplied hostname without inspecting TLS.
why: Domain fronting is possible.
check: Review allowedDomains for broad hosts where data exfiltration matters.
quote: Allowing broad domains such as `github.com` can create paths for data exfiltration.

claim: Sandbox restrictions are enforced by the OS on the running process, unlike permission decisions, which are made on command text or a classifier before it runs.
why: The boundary holds regardless of what the model chose to run.
check: Use sandbox plus permissions for defense in depth.
quote: The operating system enforces the sandbox boundary on the running process, so it holds regardless of what the model chose to run

claim: With tool search (the default) only MCP tool names and server instructions load at session start; full definitions are deferred until needed.
why: Keeps context use low as servers are added.
check: Check /context for MCP definitions loaded upfront; large upfront counts mean tool search is off or alwaysLoad is overused.
quote: Tool search keeps MCP context usage low by deferring tool definitions until Claude needs them. Only tool names and server instructions load at session start

claim: ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=auto loads MCP tools upfront while definitions total under 10% of the context window and turns deferral on at 10% or more; auto:N sets a custom percentage and false loads everything upfront.
why: Threshold mode trades startup context for fewer searches.
check: Check ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH in env and settings; false forfeits deferral.
quote: Tools that would otherwise be deferred load upfront while their definitions total under 10% of the context window.

claim: Models earlier than Opus 4, Sonnet 4 or Haiku 4.5 load all MCP tools upfront, and ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true does not override this.
why: Tool search needs model and beta support.
check: For old models or gateways expect full MCP definitions in context.
quote: On earlier models, Claude Code loads all MCP tools upfront, and `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true` doesn't override this.

claim: alwaysLoad true on a server exempts its tools from deferral and should be used only for a few tools needed every turn.
why: Each upfront tool consumes context.
check: Flag alwaysLoad on large servers.
quote: Use this for a small number of tools that Claude needs on every turn, since each upfront tool consumes context that would otherwise be available for your conversation.

claim: Server instructions and the description of an upfront-loaded MCP tool are cut at 4,096 characters, and a tool loaded via tool search at 16,384; the cut text is invisible to Claude.
why: Put critical details and search words near the start.
check: Flag MCP servers with long descriptions or instructions with essential content late.
quote: Claude Code cuts a tool description or server instructions that run past these default limits, and Claude sees only the text before the cut:

claim: Claude Code warns when an MCP tool's output exceeds 10,000 tokens and limits output to 25,000 tokens by default (MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS).
why: Protects the conversation from oversized results.
check: Check for raised MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS and servers that return large unfiltered payloads.
quote: Claude Code displays a warning when MCP tool output exceeds 10,000 tokens and limits output to 25,000 tokens by default.

claim: A successful MCP text result over 50,000 characters is saved to a file regardless of MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS, unless the tool declares anthropic/maxResultSizeChars (hard ceiling 500,000).
why: The character threshold is independent of the token limit.
check: Raising the env variable does not change the 50,000-character persistence.
quote: Claude Code saves a successful result with no image content to a file once it's longer than 50,000 characters, whatever its token count.

claim: MCP tool calls have a per-server timeout in milliseconds; values below 1000 are ignored and MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT defaults to about 28 hours, and calls running over two minutes in the main conversation move to the background.
why: Wall-clock and idle limits differ by transport.
check: Check for servers with no timeout that may hang for hours.
quote: Values below 1000 are ignored and fall through to `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT`, or to its default of about 28 hours when that variable is unset.

claim: MCP servers have local (default, per project, in ~/.claude.json), project (.mcp.json, shared) and user scopes; precedence is local, project, user, plugin, then claude.ai connectors, and the whole entry is used without merging.
why: Duplicates are resolved by name or endpoint.
check: Check for duplicate servers defined at several scopes with different settings.
quote: The entire server entry from that source is used; fields are not merged across scopes.

claim: MCP local scope stores servers in ~/.claude.json, not in .claude/settings.local.json.
why: The term local scope differs between MCP and settings.
check: Do not look for local-scope MCP servers in the project's settings.local.json.
quote: MCP local-scoped servers are stored in `~/.claude.json` (your home directory), while general local settings use `.claude/settings.local.json` (in the project directory).

claim: In -p, Agent SDK and some cloud sessions project-scoped .mcp.json servers load without an approval prompt; disabledMcpjsonServers, --setting-sources or --strict-mcp-config keep them out.
why: No prompt can be shown.
check: For automation over untrusted repos, check those exclusions.
quote: Claude Code can't show that prompt: it loads project-scoped servers without asking.

claim: A server can mark a tool with anthropic/requiresUserInteraction so it prompts on every call even in acceptEdits, auto and bypassPermissions, ignoring allow rules; dontAsk denies it.
why: For consent steps where auto-approval would remove the human.
check: Do not expect allow rules or hook allows to auto-approve such tools.
quote: Claude Code shows that tool's permission prompt on every call, even in `acceptEdits`, `auto`, and `bypassPermissions`

claim: A deployed managed-mcp.json takes exclusive control of MCP servers and suppresses claude.ai connectors unless allowAllClaudeAiMcps is set.
why: Admin exclusivity.
check: In managed environments check why expected connectors are missing.
quote: Without this key, `managed-mcp.json` takes exclusive control of MCP servers and suppresses those connectors.

claim: Claude Code leaves out an MCP tool whose full mcp__server__tool name exceeds 128 characters and excludes tools whose input schema breaks API rules, leaving the server's other tools.
why: The API rejects such tools.
check: If a tool is missing, check name length and schema validity in /mcp.
quote: Claude Code leaves an MCP tool out of the tools it sends to Claude when its full name is over 128 characters.

claim: Without tool search Claude Code does not report failed MCP server connections to Claude, so a broken server can silently vanish from its toolset.
why: With tool search it reports the failure.
check: With ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false, check servers are actually connected.
quote: Claude Code doesn't report failed server connections to Claude.

claim: Loading all MCP tool definitions upfront and routing intermediate results through the model costs tokens; presenting tools as code APIs loaded on demand cut an example from 150,000 to 2,000 tokens.
why: Definitions and large intermediate results both consume context.
check: For setups with many servers or large data passes, check for deferral, tool search or code execution.
quote: This reduces the token usage from 150,000 tokens to 2,000 tokens—a time and cost saving of 98.7%.

claim: Code execution with MCP has costs: agent-generated code needs a secure sandbox, resource limits and monitoring, to be weighed against token savings.
why: Operational overhead and security considerations.
check: Do not recommend code execution without isolation.
quote: The benefits of code execution—reduced token costs, lower latency, and improved tool composition—should be weighed against these implementation costs.

claim: Detailed tool descriptions are the most important factor in tool performance: what it does, when to use or not use it, what each parameter means, and caveats.
why: Stated by the API docs.
check: Flag one-line tool descriptions; aim for at least 3-4 sentences.
quote: This is by far the most important factor in tool performance.

claim: Each tool description should run at least three to four sentences, more for complex tools.
why: More context improves tool selection and use.
check: Count sentences in custom tool and MCP tool descriptions.
quote: Aim for at least 3–4 sentences for each tool description, more if the tool is complex.

claim: Consolidate related operations into fewer tools with an action parameter instead of one tool per action.
why: Fewer tools reduce selection ambiguity.
check: Flag tool sets with many near-duplicate narrow tools.
quote: Fewer, more capable tools reduce selection ambiguity and make your tool surface easier for Claude to navigate.

claim: Namespace tool names by service, such as github_list_prs, especially when using tool search.
why: Makes selection unambiguous as the library grows.
check: Flag generic tool names like search or list across servers.
quote: prefix names with the service (for example, `github_list_prs`, `slack_send_message`).

claim: A tool name must match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$.
why: API constraint.
check: Flag names with spaces, dots or over 128 characters.
quote: Must match the regex `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$`.

claim: input_examples must validate against the tool's input_schema or the API returns a 400.
why: Schema-validated examples.
check: Check examples match schemas; they add roughly 20-200 tokens each.
quote: Each example must be valid according to the tool’s `input_schema`. Invalid examples return a 400 error.

claim: Tool parameters should ask for an explanation or evidence, not the model's reasoning, which can trigger a reasoning_extraction refusal.
why: Stated by the docs.
check: Flag tool parameters named reasoning or thoughts.
quote: A parameter that asks for the model’s thinking or step-by-step reasoning might lead to a `reasoning_extraction` refusal.

claim: Forced tool use (tool_choice any or tool) returns a 400 on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and 5.2 and Mythos models; use auto with strict tool use instead.
why: Documented model restriction.
check: Flag tool_choice any or tool on those models.
quote: `any` and `tool` return a 400 error.

claim: Build a few tools for high-impact workflows rather than wrapping every API endpoint; overlapping tools distract agents.
why: Agents have limited context unlike software.
check: Flag servers exposing list_all style endpoints.
quote: Too many tools or overlapping tools can also distract agents from pursuing efficient strategies.

claim: Tool responses should use pagination, filtering or truncation with sensible defaults; Claude Code caps tool responses at 25,000 tokens by default.
why: Quantity of returned context matters.
check: Flag tools that return unbounded results.
quote: For Claude Code, we restrict tool responses to 25,000 tokens by default.

claim: Truncated results and errors should carry steering instructions and actionable guidance, not opaque codes or tracebacks.
why: Steers agents to token-efficient strategies.
check: Check error messages from custom tools and MCP servers.
quote: If you choose to truncate responses, be sure to steer agents with helpful instructions.

claim: Return semantically meaningful names instead of opaque UUIDs; a concise/detailed response_format enum used about a third of the tokens in the example.
why: Reduces hallucinations and tokens.
check: Flag tools returning raw IDs, mime types and internal fields.
quote: In this example, we use ~⅓ of the tokens with “concise” tool responses.

claim: Evaluate tools with realistic, multi-call tasks and verifiable outcomes, and iterate on descriptions against them.
why: Small description refinements yielded large gains.
check: Check whether any tool evaluation exists.
quote: Strong evaluation tasks might require multiple tool calls—potentially dozens.

claim: A valid Bash result reaches Claude inline up to roughly 30,000 characters; failures only roughly 10,000 characters head-and-tail with no file path.
why: Failure excerpts are smaller.
check: Check commands whose output matters on failure; and that exit 1 is not classed as failure except for grep, find, diff and test.
quote: Inline up to roughly 10,000 characters; past that, a head-and-tail excerpt of that size cut from the read-back window, with no file path

claim: A Read call returns at most 25,000 tokens by default and refuses whole files over 256 KB, so large files are read in pages.
why: Limits context spent per read.
check: Check CLAUDE_CODE_FILE_READ_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS for oversized values.
quote: By default one call returns at most 25,000 tokens, or the value you set in

claim: An Edit allow rule also grants read access to the path, and a Read deny rule also blocks Edit and Write there.
why: Both change content Claude must be able to read back.
check: Do not add redundant Read allows; a Read deny covers Edit and Write too.
quote: An `Edit(...)` allow rule also grants read access to the same path, so you don't need a matching `Read(...)` rule.
